sections.title: The 1881 Act and What Negotiable Means

blocks.title: Background of the law
items: Before 1881
The English Negotiable Instruments law applied in India
The Negotiable Instruments Act was enacted in India, based on the English Act with some modifications
RBI Act: the NI Act works subject to Sections 31 and 32 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

blocks.text: The Act extends to the whole of India. Under **Section 13(a)**, a negotiable instrument means a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer, whether or not the words ‘order’ or ‘bearer’ actually appear on the instrument.

blocks.title: Provisions about payable-to-bearer
items: A promissory note can never be made payable to the bearer, whether it is payable on demand or after a fixed time.
A bill of exchange cannot be made payable to the bearer on demand, though it can be made payable to the bearer after a certain time.
A cheque, although it is a bill of exchange, can be drawn payable to bearer on demand on a person’s account with a banker.

blocks.title: Bearer rules differ by instrument
blocks.text: Promissory note: never to bearer. Bill of exchange: not to bearer on demand (allowed after a time). Cheque: bearer on demand is allowed. The cheque is the exception because it is drawn on a banker.

blocks.title: Five characteristics
rows: The possessor is presumed to be the owner of the property in it. The instrument gives not just possession but the right to the property.
The transferee, called a holder in due course, is a bona fide transferee for value and is not affected by any defect in the title of the transferor or earlier holders.
The transferee can sue in his own name if the instrument is dishonoured. It can be transferred any number of times until maturity.
Certain presumptions apply to all instruments, such as that consideration has been paid; ‘for value received’ need not be written in a promissory note.
The holder can expect prompt payment, because dishonour ruins the credit of every party to the instrument.

blocks.title: Five traits of negotiability
blocks.phrase: Please Take Real Pearls Promptly: Property, Title, Rights, Presumptions, Prompt payment.
letters: Title: holder in due course is protected

blocks.title: Holder in due course
blocks.text: The transferee of a negotiable instrument who takes it in good faith and for value is called the holder in due course. He gets a clean title even if an earlier holder’s title was defective.
Sections 118 and 119 list the presumptions a court makes about negotiable instruments. They need not be proved; they are assumed to exist until the contrary is proved.

blocks.title: What the court presumes
rows: Every instrument was made, drawn, accepted or endorsed for consideration
A dated instrument was made or drawn on that date
An accepted bill was accepted within a reasonable time after issue and before maturity
Every transfer was made before maturity
Endorsements appear in the order in which they were made
A lost promissory note, bill or cheque was duly stamped
The holder is a holder in due course who paid consideration in good faith
On proof of protest, the court presumes the instrument was dishonoured

blocks.title: Seven presumptions of Section 118
blocks.phrase: Can Dogs Taste Tasty Orange Sweets, Honey? Consideration, Date, Time of acceptance, Time of transfer, Order of endorsement, Stamp, Holder.
blocks.note: Section 119 adds the eighth: proof of protest leads to presumption of dishonour.

blocks.text: Section 13 says a negotiable instrument is a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable to order or to bearer. These three are recognised by statute. Several others are recognised by usage or custom.

blocks.title: Statutory instruments
rows: A written instrument (not a bank-note or currency note) with an unconditional undertaking signed by the maker to pay a certain sum to a certain person, his order, or the bearer
A written instrument with an unconditional order, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum only to, or to the order of, a certain person or the bearer
A bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand

blocks.title: Sections 4, 5, 6
blocks.phrase: Section 4 = a Promise, Section 5 = a Bill, Section 6 = a Cheque: Promise, Bill, Cheque in order.
letters: Promissory note: a promise to pay
Bill of exchange: an order to pay
Cheque: a bill drawn on a banker, payable on demand

blocks.title: Instruments recognised by usage or custom
items: Hundis
Share warrants
Dividend warrants
Banker’s draft
Circular notes
Bearer debentures
Debentures of Bombay Port Trust
Railway receipts
Delivery orders

blocks.title: Nine customary instruments
blocks.phrase: Hungry Sheep Drink Black Coffee; Bears Dance, Run Daily.

blocks.title: More to know
rows: A negotiable instrument written in an oriental language; the term covers all indigenous negotiable instruments, whether in the form of notes or bills.
A cheque is a bill of exchange with two more qualifications: it is always drawn on a specified banker and always payable on demand.
Inland and foreign bills; time and demand bills; trade and accommodation bills.
Covered by the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
A negotiable financial instrument issued by a bank to represent a foreign company’s publicly traded securities.

blocks.title: Parties to a bill of exchange
rows: The person directed by the drawer to pay.
The drawee who has signed his assent on the bill and delivered it or given notice of the signing.
The person named in the instrument to whom, or to whose order, money is to be paid; the real beneficiary.
The person legally entitled to possess the instrument in his own name and to receive the amount; the payee or endorsee, or the bearer’s possessor.
A holder who transfers the instrument to someone else.
The person to whom the bill is indorsed.
A person named in addition to the drawee, to be approached if the drawee refuses; the holder must present the bill to him.
A person not liable on the bill who, with the holder’s consent, accepts it to honour a party when the drawee refuses to accept or furnish better security.

blocks.title: Parties to a promissory note and a cheque
rows: Person to whom payable; the creditor
The payee or the person to whom the note is indorsed
Draws the cheque; the depositor of money in the bank
The drawer’s banker on whom the cheque is drawn
Entitled to receive payment of the cheque

blocks.title: Who is who on a bill
blocks.phrase: The Drawer Draws, the Drawee gets Directed, once he signs he is the Acceptor, the Payee is Paid.
letters: A drawee who has signed assent
blocks.note: A promissory note has only two main parties: maker and payee.

blocks.title: Count the parties
blocks.text: A promissory note has 2 parties (maker and payee), while a bill of exchange and a cheque each start with 3 (drawer, drawee, payee).

Literally, endorsement means writing on the back of an instrument. Under the Act it means writing one’s name on the back of the instrument, or on a paper attached to it, with the intention of transferring the rights in it. The person who endorses is the **endorser**; the person to whom it is transferred is the **endorsee**.

blocks.title: Classes of endorsement
items: Blank or general
Special or full
Partial
Restrictive
Conditional

blocks.title: Transfer by signing
blocks.text: Transferring an instrument to another person by signing on its back or face, or on a slip of paper attached to it, is endorsement.

sections.title: Lost, Stolen, Fraudulent and Forged Instruments

blocks.text: A person cannot pass a better title than he himself has. A finder of lost goods, a thief, or someone who gets a thing by fraud or for an unlawful consideration gets no title to it. Negotiable instruments differ from ordinary goods in how title passes, but the basic rule stays for the following cases.

blocks.title: Defective title cases
rows: The finder gets no title and cannot lawfully transfer it; the loser can recover it from the finder
The thief is in the same position as a finder; he gets no title, and if he receives payment the owner can sue him to recover the amount
Consent obtained by fraud makes the contract voidable at the option of the person defrauded; the fraudster gets a defective title
An instrument given for an illegal consideration is void and conveys no valid title to the holder
Forgery confers no title; a forged instrument is treated as a nullity

blocks.title: Forgery with intent to gain title includes
items: Fraudulently writing the name of an existing person.
Signing the name of a fictitious person with the intention that it may pass as that of a real person.
Signing one’s own name intending it to pass as the signature of another person of the same name.

blocks.title: Five ways title goes wrong
blocks.phrase: Lazy Thieves Find Unlawful Forgeries: Lost, Stolen, Fraud, Unlawful consideration, Forged.
letters: Lost instrument: finder has no title
Stolen instrument: thief has no title

blocks.text: When an instrument is dishonoured, the holder must give notice of dishonour to the earlier parties he wants to make liable. An instrument can be dishonoured by **non-acceptance** or by **non-payment**. A cheque and a promissory note can be dishonoured only by non-payment, but a bill of exchange can be dishonoured either way.

blocks.title: Sections to remember
rows: Notice of dishonour: who gives it to the prior parties
Instrument overdue and unpaid when presentment for payment is excused

blocks.title: Dishonour of a bill by non-acceptance (Section 91)
items: The drawee does not accept within 48 hours of presentment. If there are several drawees, one default means dishonour, unless they are partners (acceptance by one then binds all).
The drawee is a fictitious person or cannot be traced after reasonable search.
The drawee is incompetent to contract.
The bill is accepted with a qualified acceptance; the holder may treat it as dishonoured.
The drawee has become insolvent or is dead.
Presentment for acceptance is excused and the bill is not accepted. If a drawee in case of need is named, the bill is not dishonoured until he also refuses.

blocks.title: Non-payment, effect and notice
rows: An accepted bill must be presented for payment on its maturity date; if the acceptor fails to pay, it is dishonoured by non-payment.
Other parties can be made liable; for example, if the acceptor dishonours, the holder may sue the drawer and the indorsers.
Actual notification of dishonour by non-acceptance or non-payment, to be given immediately to the parties the holder wants to make liable.
The holder or a party liable on it gives notice to all prior parties he wants to hold liable; notice may also go to a party’s agent.

blocks.title: Sections 91, 92, 93
blocks.phrase: 91 Acceptance, 92 Payment, 93 Notice: A-P-N in a row.
blocks.note: Cheque and note: only non-payment. Bill: both, so it has two doors to dishonour.

revision: The Negotiable Instruments Act was enacted in 1881 and is based on the English Act; it extends to the whole of India.
Section 13(a): a negotiable instrument is a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable to order or bearer.
A promissory note can never be made payable to the bearer.
A bill of exchange cannot be payable to bearer on demand; a cheque payable to bearer on demand is allowed.
Section 4 defines a promissory note, Section 5 a bill of exchange and Section 6 a cheque.
Statutory instruments: promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques; hundis, share warrants and others are recognised by custom.
A cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and payable on demand.
A holder in due course takes the instrument in good faith and for value and gets a clean title.
Sections 118 and 119 lay down presumptions such as consideration, date, order of endorsement and holder in due course.
A promissory note has two parties, the maker and the payee.
Endorsement is of five classes: blank, special, partial, restrictive and conditional.
A finder or thief gets no title to a negotiable instrument; a forged instrument is a nullity.
Cheques and promissory notes can be dishonoured only by non-payment; bills by non-acceptance or non-payment.
Section 91 deals with dishonour by non-acceptance, Section 92 non-payment and Section 93 notice of dishonour.
A drawee who does not accept within 48 hours of presentment has dishonoured the bill.
